title: Sioux Falls, a Twin City dust-up, and a bus ride
contentHtml:
I wasn’t sure what the young man wanted; he was shouting and pointing behind me, but all I heard was car engines. Was there a fire? An accident? Nope, he wanted to make sure I saw “the most beautiful sky ever.” I hadn’t, and I had to agree with him, it was majestic, a poetic contrast to our circumstance — sitting on a retaining wall next to eight lanes of traffic, amid interchangeable box stores with garish advertising.

Landon is as gregarious as I am curious, so I got the full account of his eighteen years on this earth as we waited for the bus, he headed home from his shift at the thrift store, me to dinner. His temperament matched the sunset — luminous despite a tumultuous setting. So I heard about his future plans (college, wrestling scholarship, game design), and about a mother, who, while “physically alive,” died to him years before. She was an addict, who “did everything bad that a mother could do,” consuming “every drug but the ones that would kill her.” Her addiction, and a biological father he knew little about, are why he doesn’t touch anything — “doesn’t drink, smoke, vape, or any of that” — or plan to.

Landon’s strident optimism fit Sioux Falls — a city that immediately impressed me with its confidence, an effusiveness kept from spinning into silliness by its practicality. As with the Midwest surrounding it, that practicality is rooted in producing tangible things — in Sioux Falls's case, servicing the people who grow, raise, and slaughter the food we eat.

It’s not a picturesque city, at least not the part where I met Landon and spent my first days. My room was in a fifty-dollar-a-night hotel adjacent to a McDonald’s, a stone’s throw from a Walmart superstore — all three inside a four-square-mile triangle of commerce wedged against interstates that, while legally in Sioux Falls, SD, could be Anywhere, USA.

Every major franchise exists within the triangle (Menards, Sam’s Club, Starbucks, Buffalo Wild Wings, Home Depot, Barnes & Noble, etc.) as well as larval chains hoping to strike it big (Slim Chickens, etc.), and several lingering in franchise purgatory (Granite City Food & Brewery).

It is a self-contained community with everything anyone could want inside, including faith (C6 Church, The Light of the World, Assemblies of God) and plenty of sin (Blazin Aces, Chasing Clouds, Holy Smokes, Scarlett O’Hara’s Gentlemen’s Club, Empire Casino, etc.). While it lacks housing, enough out-of-state workers live for months in its dozens of hotels to count as residents. All it needs is a branding acronym, like TriBeSku — Triangle Below Skunk Creek.

The big event during my TriBeSku residency was the grand opening of a Raising Cane’s, which brought block-long drive-through lines, timed entry, and security guards in high-vis vests. It also increased TriBeSku’s fall population, with over fifty Raising Cane’s employees flown in earlier from Vegas to make sure the launch went without a hitch. This wasn’t surprising. As one man my age told me, “We get giddy here about new stuff coming. Was same when Chipotle first opened up.”

I was content with my time in TriBeSku, despite not having a car and it being entirely about having a car. These modern conglomerations of franchises that lie along the outer edges of every US city — the neighborhoods of parking lots, access roads, engorged block buildings, and forests of fluorescent signs — are the logical end point of our vehicular monotheism. They are the Lego towers we build from our basic urban building brick — the drive-through1.

You cannot talk about modern America if you ignore them, because they are the new downtowns, which is why I decided to stay in TriBeSku, but as I soon discovered I couldn’t have chosen a worse city than Sioux Falls to make that point.

That's because when I finally moved to a central hotel, for a weekend conference, I was charmed beyond all expectations — Sioux Falls downtown is lovely, bucking the national trend of city centers declining into depressing shells of vape stores, tattoo parlors, bail-bond shops, and for-rent signs, with only municipal business to prop them up. While small (effectively five square blocks) it has a wealth of private businesses (architects, lawyers, banks, corporate headquarters) in glamorous buildings, wonderful bespoke stores -- bakeries, cafes, retail, bars, restaurants -- and a night scene that lingers into the following morning.

Precisely why Sioux Falls has maintained a thriving downtown, despite the competing growth at its edges, despite an economy shifting away from office hubs, is beyond the scope of this essay, but it’s clear that it’s been a decades-long priority of community leaders, and now is a source of pride for its citizens. Sioux-fall-ers2 respect their downtown, a destination distinct from TriBeSku by its charm, and the idea of littering in it, or misbehaving in it, is seen as akin to talking in church. Something you don’t do, regardless of whether you will be caught.

I was especially sensitive to all of this because of my earlier experience in the Twin Cities. I’d come to Minneapolis to meet some readers (thanks to everyone for showing up!), and then catch a bus to Sioux Falls, not to write about it, but with two empty days I went on long walks, one from downtown Minneapolis to St. Paul. Against my better judgement I posted my immediate thoughts on Twitter3, the primary thrust of those posts being I was struck by how sad it was to find two McDonald’s with completely shuttered dining rooms, and how despondent and empty the downtowns were, especially that of St. Paul. I also mentioned how glorious the Cathedral of Saint Paul is, but that was ignored in the social media storm that followed.

I’d intentionally stayed away from writing about the Twin Cities before, given that they’d become a political football to fight over, a place for “influencers” to try and get influence from, by maliciously and disingenuously hyping Y (insert issue of day) on X (your social media of choice). That’s not my style, or at least I don’t intend it to be.

Yet here I was stepping right into the middle of a maelstrom, something I should have known better than to do. I’d wrongly assumed the recent elections had lowered the temperature, but memory is slow to fade, and Minneapolis is a political town, with a long legacy of left-leaning progressivism, from the Grangers of the Gilded Age to today’s DFL, for our current Gilded Age reboot. That has made it an escape destination for left-leaning activists drawn from across the conservative rural Midwest, and consequently it’s become a convenient target for today’s red politicians and influencers.
